sections.content: Teaching a {term:model:model} by showing it thousands of example conversations. Like a student copying "ideal" homework - the {term:model:model} learns to produce responses that look like the training examples. Effective for teaching FORMAT but limited because it just copies patterns rather than learning what makes a response GOOD.
Supervised learning on (instruction, response) pairs. Minimizes cross-entropy {term:loss:loss} on response {term:token:tokens} only.

sections.title: Training Example
sections.content:
Data: {instruction: "Explain gravity", response: "Imagine invisible strings..."}

Process: Feed both as sequence → {term:model:Model} predicts response tokens → {term:loss:Loss} only on response → Update {term:theta:weights}

Instead of copying responses, {term:model:model} GENERATES its own and gets scored. A {term:reward:reward} {term:model:model} (trained on preferences) scores it. Learning from a coach, not copying textbooks.
{term:policy:Policy} optimization with learned {term:reward:reward} + {term:kl:KL} penalty to stay near {term:sft:SFT} baseline.

sections.title: Flow
sections.content:
1. Collect preferences: Human says B > A
2. Train {term:reward:reward} {term:model:model}: R(B-like) = 0.85, R(A-like) = 0.20
3. RL: Generate → Score → Update {term:theta:weights}
Automated verification instead of human preferences. For math: calculator. For code: unit tests. {term:reward:Reward} is binary: RIGHT (1.0) or WRONG (0.0). No humans, scales infinitely.
Binary {term:reward:reward} from deterministic verifiers. No neural {term:reward:reward} {term:model:model}.

sections.title: Verification
sections.content:
Math: "847 × 23 = 19481" → calculator → TRUE → R=1.0
Code: is_prime → run_tests → pass → R=1.0
Limit: Only verifiable tasks
Raw pre-trained LLM. Predicts "what comes next" but doesn't know to ANSWER or refuse harmful. Ask "What is 2+2?" → might say "What is 2+3?" (completion mode).
Next-{term:token:token} prediction on web data. No task-specific optimization.

sections.title: Behavior
sections.content:
Examples: LLaMA-2 Base, GPT-3 davinci-base
Problem: Learned helpful tutorials AND harmful content without knowing which to use

slides.title: What Does SFT Actually Do? (The Copying Teacher)

content.title: The Setup
content.content:
You have a pre-trained LLM that can complete text but doesn't follow instructions. Ask it "What is 2+2?" → it might respond "What is 2+3? What is 2+4?" (completion, not answering).

{term:sft:SFT}'s job: Teach the {term:model:model} that when a human asks a question, you ANSWER it.

content.title: What {term:sft:SFT} Data Looks Like
content.content:
Thousands of (instruction, ideal_response) pairs. Typically 10K-100K examples.

Example entry:
• instruction: "Explain gravity to a 5-year-old"
• response: "Imagine everything has invisible strings pulling it toward the ground..."

Sources: Human writers, GPT-4 generations, filtered web data.

content.title: How {term:sft:SFT} Training Works
content.content:
Step 1: Feed instruction + response as one sequence
• Example: "[INST] Explain gravity [/INST] Imagine everything has invisible strings..."

Step 2: {term:model:Model} predicts each {term:token:token}, gets {term:loss:loss} ONLY on response {term:token:tokens}
• Instruction tokens: NO {term:loss:loss}
• Response tokens: {term:loss:Loss} computed

Step 3: For token "Imagine", if {term:model:model} predicted P("Imagine") = 0.02
• {term:loss:Loss} = -log(0.02) = 3.9 (HIGH!)
• Update {term:theta:weights} to increase P("Imagine")

Step 4: Repeat millions of times

content.title: What {term:sft:SFT} Actually Does
content.content:
Before: Text predictor. "What is 2+2?" → "What is 2+3?"
After: Learns PATTERN: [instruction] → [helpful response]

The catch: {term:sft:SFT} copies training responses verbatim.

If training has 50 gravity explanations with different metaphors, the {term:model:model} learns the AVERAGE. It doesn't learn "what's BEST" - just "what appeared in training".

content.title: The {term:sft:SFT} Problem
content.content:
Research (ICML 2025): On out-of-distribution tests, {term:sft:SFT} drops -8% to -79%

Example: Train on 2-digit multiplication → Test on 3-digit → Fails

The {term:model:model} memorized patterns, not principles.

This is why we need RL: to learn STRATEGY, not copy patterns.
Want deeper {term:sft:SFT} details? See our Training & Fine-Tuning LLMs topic.

slides.title: What Does RL Actually Do? (The Scoring Coach)

content.title: The Key Difference
content.content:
{term:sft:SFT}: "Here's a perfect response. Copy it exactly."
RL: "Generate whatever you want. I'll tell you how good it was. Do better next time."

{term:sft:SFT} = learning from textbook.
RL = learning from coach who grades performance.

content.title: RL Training Loop
content.content:
There IS no fixed dataset. The {term:model:model} generates its own training {term:data:data}!

1. Prompt: "Explain quantum physics simply"
2. {term:model:Model} generates multiple responses
   • A: "Particles can be waves..." → {term:reward:R} = 0.73
   • B: "Imagine tiny balls..." → {term:reward:R} = 0.89 ← Best!
   • C: "Quantum mechanics states..." → {term:reward:R} = 0.62
3. Update: Make {term:model:model} more likely to generate B-like responses

The {term:model:model} explores and learns which STRATEGIES work.

content.title: Step-by-Step RL Training
content.content:
Step 1 - Generate:
• Prompt: "What is 12 × 15?" → Response: "Let me calculate: 180"

Step 2 - Score:
• {term:rlhf:RLHF}: Neural {term:reward:reward} {term:model:model} → {term:reward:R} = 0.78
• {term:rlvr:RLVR}: Rule verifier → {term:reward:R} = 1.0 (correct!)

Step 3 - Advantage:
• Was this better than expected? {term:advantage:A} = 0.78 - 0.65 = +0.13

Step 4 - Update:
• Increase {term:probability:P} of {term:token:tokens} that led to high {term:reward:reward}
• {term:kl:KL} penalty keeps {term:model:model} from drifting too far from {term:sft:SFT}

content.title: Why RL Generalizes Better
content.content:
{term:sft:SFT}: "Problems like X → responses like Y"
RL: "Doing Z gets high {term:reward:rewards}. Do more Z."

Math example:
• {term:sft:SFT}: Copies "23×17=391"
• RL: Discovers strategies that transfer:
   • Break into steps: 23×17 = 23×10 + 23×7 = 391
   • Verify: "391/23 = 17 "

{term:sft:SFT} memorized one answer. RL found transferable strategy.

Result: RL shows +3% to +61% on out-of-distribution tasks.

content.title: The {term:kl:KL} Penalty - Why We Need a Leash
content.content:
Problem: Without constraints, RL can "hack" the {term:reward:reward} {term:model:model}.
• "AMAZING! PERFECT! WOW!" × 50 → {term:reward:R} = 0.99 (oops)

Solution: {term:kl:KL} penalty keeps {term:model:model} near {term:sft:SFT} baseline

explanation.template: β controls the leash: β=0 (no leash, chaos), β=0.1 (explore reasonably), β=1.0 (tight). Typical: β ∈ [0.01, 0.1]

slides.title: What is Alignment? (Teaching the Model VALUES)

content.title: The Problem Alignment Solves
content.content:
A pre-trained LLM predicts "what comes next" from internet {term:data:data}.

Internet includes: helpful tutorials, racist rants, misinformation, malware, scams...

The {term:model:model} learned ALL of it. Ask "how to make a bomb?" and it might tell you.

Alignment = Teaching which knowledge to USE vs REFUSE.

content.title: Two Types of Alignment
content.content:
Type A: Preference ({term:rlhf:RLHF})
• Goal: Helpful, harmless, honest
• Domain: Chatbots, assistants
• {term:reward:Reward}: Learned from human preferences

Type B: Reasoning ({term:rlvr:RLVR})
• Goal: CORRECT for verifiable tasks
• Domain: Math, code, logic
• {term:reward:Reward}: Binary from automated verifiers

{term:rlhf:RLHF} = "don't be harmful" | {term:rlvr:RLVR} = "get right answer"

content.title: {term:rlhf:RLHF}: Human Preference Alignment
content.content:
Step 1 - Collect Preferences:
• Prompt: "Best way to lose weight?"
• A: "Diet pills! Lose 30 lbs fast!" | B: "Gradual diet/exercise changes..."
• Human: B is better (safer)

Step 2 - Train {term:reward:Reward} Model:
• Learns: {term:reward:R}(B-like) = 0.85, {term:reward:R}(A-like) = 0.20

Step 3 - RL: Generate → Score → Learn to generate B-like

Issues: $$$ for humans, subjective, can be gamed

content.title: {term:rlvr:RLVR}: Verifiable Rewards
content.content:
No humans for scoring!

Math: "847 × 23 = ?" → "19,481" → calculator.check() → TRUE → {term:reward:R}=1.0

Code: is_prime() → run_tests([2→True, 4→False]) → pass → {term:reward:R}=1.0

Why powerful: No annotation cost, objective, scales infinitely
Limit: Only verifiable tasks. Can't verify "is essay good?"

content.title: Pipeline 1: Standard ({term:base-model:Base} → {term:sft:SFT} → RL)
content.content:
Stage 1: Pre-training (done for you)
• Start with LLaMA, Mistral. Already knows language.

Stage 2: {term:sft:SFT} (teaches FORMAT)
• Input: 10K-100K (instruction, response) pairs
• Learns: "Answer questions", "Use markdown", "Be polite"
• Does NOT learn what's BEST

Stage 3: RL (teaches STRATEGY)
• Input: Prompts + {term:reward:reward} signal
• Learns: "Detailed explanations score higher", "Verify math", "Refuse harmful"

Why two stages? {term:sft:SFT} gives RL stable starting point.

content.title: Pipeline 2: Pure RL (DeepSeek-R1-Zero)
content.content:
Experiment: Skip {term:sft:SFT}? Just RL on {term:base-model:base model}?

What worked:
• Reasoning emerged ("think step by step")
• Self-verification appeared
• Matched o1 on math

Problems:
• Language mixing (English → Chinese mid-sentence)
• Alien formatting (no markdown)
• Phrase repetition
• MASSIVE compute needed

Conclusion: RL CAN work alone, but {term:sft:SFT} provides stability.

content.title: Pipeline 3: DeepSeek-R1 (4-Stage Production)
content.content:
Stage 1: Cold-Start {term:sft:SFT}
• ~1K reasoning examples. Just enough to prevent chaos.

Stage 2: Reasoning RL (GRPO)
• Math/code with verifiable {term:reward:rewards}. Develops chain-of-thought.

Stage 3: Rejection Sampling
• Generate millions, keep correct + readable + good format
• Result: 800K high-quality examples

Stage 4: Full {term:sft:SFT} + {term:rlhf:RLHF}
• Fine-tune on 800K, then {term:rlhf:RLHF} for safety

Result: R1-Zero's reasoning + normal readability

content.title: The Forgetting Problem
content.content:
Issue: RL after {term:sft:SFT} can "forget" what {term:sft:SFT} taught

Example:
• {term:sft:SFT} teaches: "Use markdown"
• RL optimizes: "Get high {term:reward:reward}"
• Result: Stops using markdown ({term:reward:reward} {term:model:model} doesn't care)

This is "Alignment Tax" - improving one hurts another.

content.title: Emerging: Joint Training (BRIDGE)
content.content:
Instead of {term:sft:SFT}-then-RL, do BOTH simultaneously:

Combined objective: {term:loss:Loss} = SFT_loss + λ × RL_loss

• {term:sft:SFT} keeps teaching format
• RL keeps improving strategy
• They inform each other continuously

Still research-stage, but promising.

content.title: Pipeline Summary
content.content:
Pathway 1: Standard (Stable)
• {term:base-model:Base} → {term:sft:SFT} → RL
• Examples: GPT-4, Claude, Llama-3

Pathway 2: Pure RL (Experimental)
• {term:base-model:Base} → RL only
• Example: DeepSeek-R1-Zero
• Emergent reasoning but unstable

Pathway 3: 4-Stage (Production)
• {term:base-model:Base} → Cold {term:sft:SFT} → RL → Rejection Sampling → Full {term:sft:SFT}/{term:rlhf:RLHF}
• Example: DeepSeek-R1

Pathway 4: Joint (Research)
• {term:base-model:Base} → {term:sft:SFT} + RL together
• Examples: BRIDGE, UFT
